{{Short description|Nonlinear second-order partial differential equation of special kind}}
{{confuse|Monge equation}}

In [[mathematics]], a (real) '''Monge–Ampère equation''' is a nonlinear second-order [[partial differential equation]] of special kind. A second-order equation for the unknown function <math>u</math> of two variables <math>x</math>, <math>y</math> is of Monge–Ampère type if it is linear in the [[determinant]] of the [[Hessian matrix]] of <math>u</math> and in the second-order [[partial derivative]]s of <math>u</math>. The independent variables (<math>x</math>, <math>y</math>) vary over a given domain <math>D</math> of <math>\R^2</math>. The term also applies to analogous equations with <math>n</math> independent variables. The most complete results so far have been obtained when the equation is [[elliptic operator|elliptic]].

It is named after [[Gaspard Monge]] who introduced [[descriptive geometry]] and the first form of the partial differential equation in 1784,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Monge |first=Gaspard |date=1784 |title=Mémoire sur le calcul intégral des équations aux différences partielles |journal=Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences |language=fr}}</ref> and after [[André-Marie Ampère]] who introduced the nonlinear partial differential equation in 1820<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ampère |first=André-Marie |title=Mémoire contenant l'application de la théorie exposée dans le XVII. e Cahier du Journal de l'École polytechnique, à l'intégration des équations aux différentielles partielles du premier et du second ordre |date=1819 |publisher=Imprimerie royale, 1819 |publication-place=Paris, France |language=fr}}</ref> when studying the geometry of surfaces.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Arendt |first1=Wolfgang |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z9ekEAAAQBAJ&dq=Monge-Amp%C3%A8re+equation+%22Gaspard+Monge%22+1784&pg=PA20 |title=Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction to Analytical and Numerical Methods |last2=Urban |first2=Karsten |date=2023-01-01 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-13379-4 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Luis Caffarelli]] earned the 2023 [[Abel Prize]] for his work on this equation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vázquez |first=Juan Luis |date=2024-06-19 |title=Luis Caffarelli, winner of the Abel Prize 2023 |url=https://euromathsoc.org/magazine/articles/192 |journal=European Mathematical Society Magazine |language=en |issue=132 |pages=14–22 |doi=10.4171/mag/192 |doi-access=free |issn=2747-7894}}</ref>

== Definition ==

=== In two dimension ===
Given two independent variables <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, and one dependent variable <math>u</math>, the general Monge–Ampère equation is of the form

:<math>
\begin{align}
L[u] =& A \det(\nabla^2 u) + B \Delta u + 2 C u_{xy} + (D-B) u_{yy} + E            \\
     =& A(u_{xx} u_{yy} - u_{xy}^2) + B u_{xx} + 2 C u_{xy} + D u_{yy} + E 
     =  0,
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>, <math>D</math>, and <math>E</math> are functions depending on the variables <math>x</math>, <math>y</math>, <math>u</math>, <math>u_x</math>, and <math>u_y</math> only.

=== In general ===
Given a domain <math>\Omega \subset \R^n</math> and a real-valued function <math>u \colon \Omega \to \R</math>, a (real) Monge–Ampère equation is any fully nonlinear second-order equation that can be written in the form
:<math>F(x,u,Du,\det D^2 u) = 0,</math>
for some function <math>F</math>. More generally, <math>\Omega</math> can be a [[Riemannian manifold]], since <math>Du, D^2 u </math> are well-defined on a Riemannian manifold.

If <math>F</math> also depends linearly on all principal minors of the Hessian matrix <math>D^2 u</math>, then it is an '''equation of Monge–Ampère type'''.

=== Classification ===
{{Main|Elliptic partial differential equation#Nonlinear and higher-order equations}}
As for other second-order fully nonlinear equations, the type of a Monge–Ampère equation is defined by the [[linearization]] of the operator at a sufficiently smooth solution. Of these, the most common is the elliptic case. When people say "Monge–Ampère equation" without adjective, they usually mean the elliptic case.

Let <math>\Omega \subset \R^n</math> be an [[open set]], <math>u \colon \Omega \to \R</math> be a <math>C^2</math> function, and consider an operator of Monge–Ampère type
:<math>L[u] = F(x,u,Du,D^2 u),</math>
where <math>F</math> is smooth in all variables and depends on <math>D^2 u</math> only through its principal minors. The linearization of <math>L</math> is of form
:<math>\sum_{ij} a^{ij}(x)\,u_{ij} + \text{lower order terms},</math>
where
:<math>a^{ij}(x) = \frac{\partial F}{\partial u_{ij}}(x,u(x),Du(x),D^2 u(x)).</math>
The [[quadratic form]]
:<math>Q_x(\xi) = a^{ij}(x)\,\xi_i \xi_j,\qquad \xi \in \R^n,</math>
is the principal symbol of the linearized operator at the point <math>x</math>.

The equation is said to be
* '''elliptic at <math>x</math>''' if <math>Q_x(\xi)</math> if all eigenvalues are of the same sign,
* '''hyperbolic at <math>x</math>''' if <math>Q_x(\xi)</math> takes both positive and negative values (the matrix is indefinite),
* '''parabolic at <math>x</math>''' if <math>Q_x(\xi)</math> is degenerate (the matrix has vanishing determinant),
* '''degenerate elliptic''' if it is elliptic everywhere,
* '''elliptic''' if it is degenerate elliptic, and all eigenvalues are a bounded distance away from zero.

As follows from [[Jacobi's formula]] for the derivative of a determinant, this equation is elliptic if <math>f</math> is a positive function and solutions satisfy the constraint of being [[uniformly convex]]. If <math>f</math> is merely [[Strictly convex function|''strictly'' convex]], then the equation is degenerate-elliptic.{{sfnm|1a1=Gilbarg|1a2=Trudinger|1y=2001|location=Chap. 17}}

== Examples ==
The Monge–Ampère equation in its simplest form is
:<math>\det D^2 u = f(x)</math>
where <math>f</math> is a given function on a domain <math>\Omega \subset \R^n</math>. This is a special case of equation (1) below with <math>f(x,u,Du) = f(x)</math>.

The classical [[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville theorem]] has an analogy here. If <math>\det D^2 u</math> is constant, and <math>u</math> is defined on all of <math>\R^n</math>, then <math>u</math> is a [[quadratic function]]. This is the '''Jörgens–Calabi–Pogorelov theorem'''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Figalli |first=Alessio |title=The Monge-Ampère equation and its applications |date=2017 |publisher=European Mathematical Society |isbn=978-3-03719-170-5 |series=Zurich lectures in advanced mathematics |location=Zürich}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Sec. 4.3}}

If <math>f(x)</math> is positive and uniformly convex, and <math>u</math> is a solution to <math>\det D^2 u = f(x)</math>, then its [[Legendre transformation|Legendre transform]] <math>u^*</math> is a solution to <math>\det D^2 u^* = 1/f(x)</math>.

=== Geometry ===
Monge–Ampère equations arise naturally in several problems in [[Riemannian geometry]], [[conformal geometry]], [[Affine differential geometry|affine geometry]], and [[CR geometry]].

Given a twice-differentiable real-valued function <math>f: \Omega \to \R</math> defined over a domain <math>\Omega \subset \R^n</math>, its [[Graph of a function|graph]] is a manifold of ''n'' dimensions. At any <math>x \in \Omega</math>, the [[Gaussian curvature]] of the manifold at <math>f(x)</math> is <math>\frac{\det D^2 u}{(1 + |Du|^2)^{(n+2)/2}}</math>. Thus, if we want to find a manifold whose Gaussian curvature is an arbitrary function we pick ourselves, then we need to solve the following Monge–Ampère equation:
:<math>\det D^2 u - K(x)(1 + |Du|^2)^{(n+2)/2} = 0</math>
where <math>K</math> is the Gaussian curvature we want. Given such a function K, it is nontrivial to find a solution, if any. The problem of finding a solution is the '''[[Hermann Minkowski|Minkowski]] problem''', or the '''prescribed Gaussian curvature problem'''.{{sfnm|1a1=Gilbarg|1a2=Trudinger|1y=2001}}

For example, the rigidity of the 2-sphere manifests as the fact that if we require <math>n = 3, K = 1, u(0) = 0, Du = 0</math>, then there are just two unique solutions, which is the unit 2-sphere and its reflection.

The [[Affine sphere|affine spheres]] can be characterized by a Monge–Ampère equation.

=== Optimal transport ===
Consider the problem of [[optimal transport]] with quadratic cost (this is also called the [[Wasserstein metric|2-Wasserstein metric]] problem) on <math>\R^n</math>. That is, suppose <math>\mu, \nu</math> are distributions on <math>\R^n</math> with probability density functions <math>\rho_\mu, \rho_\nu</math>. In this case, a map <math>T : \operatorname{supp}(\mu) \to \operatorname{supp}(\nu)</math> is a transport map iff it satisfies<math display="block">\int h(T(x)) \rho_\mu(x) dx = \int h(y) \rho_\nu(y) dy</math>for any integrable test function <math>h \in L^1(\operatorname{supp}(\nu))</math>. The problem is to find the <math>T</math> that minimizes the following quadratic cost function:<math display="block">\min_T \int \|x - T(x) \|^2 f(x) dx</math>By a theorem of Brenier, the optimal transport map exists, and is the gradient of a convex function <math>\psi: \operatorname{supp}(\mu) \to \R^n</math>, with <math>T = D \psi</math>. The convex function satisfies a [[Monge–Ampère equation]]:{{sfnm|1a1=Villani|1y=2009}}{{Reference page|page=282}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Prins |first1=C. R. |last2=Beltman |first2=R. |last3=ten Thije Boonkkamp |first3=J. H. M. |last4=IJzerman |first4=W. L. |last5=Tukker |first5=T. W. |date=January 2015 |title=A Least-Squares Method for Optimal Transport Using the Monge--Ampère Equation |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/140986414 |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |language=en |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=B937–B961 |doi=10.1137/140986414 |bibcode=2015SJSC...37B.937P |issn=1064-8275}}</ref>{{sfnm|1a1=Villani|1y=2003|2a1=Villani|2y=2009}}<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\det(D^2 \psi) = \frac{\rho_\mu}{\rho_\nu \circ D \psi}\\
D \psi(\partial\operatorname{supp}(\mu)) = \partial \operatorname{supp}(\nu)
\end{cases}</math>The boundary condition simply states that the optimal transport maps the boundary of the source to the boundary of the target. Furthermore, the solution <math>\psi</math> is almost everywhere unique. 

The function <math>\psi</math> is called the '''potential function''' of the problem in this case.

Conversely, some Monge–Ampère equations can be interpreted optimal transport. Weak-solutions of a Monge–Ampère equations obtained by optimal transport are often called '''Brenier solutions''' in the literature. Brenier solutions satisfy their corresponding Monge–Ampère equations almost everywhere.{{sfnm|1a1=Villani|1y=2009}}{{Reference page|page=323}}

== Rellich's theorem ==
Let <math>\Omega</math> be a bounded domain in <math>\R^3</math>, and suppose that on <math>\Omega</math> the coefficients <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math>, <math>D</math>, and <math>E</math> are continuous functions of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> only. Consider the [[Dirichlet problem]] to find <math>u</math> so that

:<math>L[u]=0,\quad \text{on}\ \Omega</math>
:<math>u|_{\partial\Omega}=g.</math>

If

:<math>BD-C^2-AE > 0,</math>

then the Dirichlet problem has at most two solutions.{{sfnm|1a1=Courant|1a2=Hilbert|1y=1962|1p=324}}

== Ellipticity results ==
Suppose now that <math>\mathbf{x}</math> is a variable with values in a domain in <math>\R^n</math>, and that <math>f(\mathbf{x},u,Du)</math> is a positive function. Then the Monge–Ampère equation

:<math>L[u] = \det D^2 u - f(\mathbf{x},u,Du)=0\qquad\qquad (1)</math>

is a [[nonlinear equation|nonlinear]] [[elliptic partial differential equation]] (in the sense that its [[linearization]] is elliptic), provided one confines attention to [[convex function|convex]] solutions.

Accordingly, the operator <math>L</math> satisfies versions of the [[maximum principle]], and in particular solutions to the Dirichlet problem are unique, provided they exist.{{citation needed|date=May 2014}}
